video_title: The Future Of Money Panel | Peter Schiff, Brent Johnson, Dominic Frisby & Russ Gray
gist: At the New Orleans Investment Conference panel, Peter Schiff, Brent Johnson, Dominic Frisby and Russ Gray debate structurally higher rates, financial repression and sovereign debt, with Johnson arguing dollar stablecoins extend dollar dominance (other fiat fails first) and Schiff countering that rates must rise far further and gold is the real money. Consensus: own real/productive assets, equities and gold.

insights.claim: Dominic Frisby argues the 2020 sub-1% yield low marked a 40-year secular bottom (from the 1980 high) and a new cycle of structurally more expensive fiat capital has begun, though rates may pull back short term.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Position for secularly higher yields; treat rallies in long bonds as counter-trend, and stress-test capital-intensive businesses for higher funding costs.
insights.quote: I think 2020 whenever when rates went below 1% that was the low that was a secular low.

insights.claim: Peter Schiff says the current rise in yields is not transitory but a return to normal after the post-2008 aberration, and that rates 'have a long way to rise' because sovereign creditworthiness is far worse than 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the mainstream 'transitory' view; implies avoiding long-duration Treasuries and expecting term premium to keep widening.
insights.quote: the normalization of rates is just getting started. Rates have a long way to rise from here.

insights.claim: Schiff argues that because asset prices (houses, stocks) were reset on artificially low rates, normalizing rates toward levels consistent with the debt load will trigger a crisis the economy cannot handle.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive asset valuations (real estate, long-duration equities) are vulnerable as rates reset higher.
insights.quote: All of our asset prices, houses, stocks, the whole economy has now been reset based on these artificially low rates.

insights.claim: Schiff assigns a nonzero probability to an outright US default and argues the $40.5 trillion national debt is only the tip of an iceberg of tens of trillions in unfunded promises (Social Security, government pensions, Medicare); the honest alternative to hyperinflation is cutting benefits and haircutting bondholders alike.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Treasury holders should not assume they are senior to entitlement claimants; sovereign credit risk is being underpriced in his view.
insights.quote: the $40 and half trillion dollar national debt is the tip of a huge debt iceberg

insights.claim: Schiff blames central bankers more than legislators for the debt predicament because they enabled government profligacy instead of 'taking the punch bowl away', and says the Fed under the current chair (Warsh) behaves the same as under Powell, Yellen and Bernanke.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Do not expect Fed leadership changes to deliver real monetary discipline; inflation-hedge positioning stays warranted.
insights.quote: The Fed is really behaving exactly the same as it did under Worsh.

insights.claim: Schiff dismisses a 125 basis point rate hike as meaningless relative to the price inflation being experienced.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Signals he views policy as still behind the curve; real rates likely remain inadequate to defend purchasing power.
insights.quote: 125 basis point rate hike is meaningless

insights.claim: Schiff recalls Janet Yellen, as Treasury Secretary, saying the debt was affordable because rates were low, and argues that premise collapses as rates inevitably rise, making debt service unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Watch federal interest expense as a share of revenue; rising rates directly worsen the fiscal arithmetic.

insights.claim: Schiff frames rising consumer costs (groceries, gas, insurance) as a hidden tax caused by the rising cost of government financed via inflation rather than explicit taxation.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Fiscal expansion financed by money creation shows up in cost of living; favors real-asset hedges over cash.
insights.quote: People are now experiencing the cost of government every time they go to the store.

insights.claim: Frisby expects governments, as the largest borrowers, to suppress their borrowing costs via another round of quantitative easing, but predicts it will be less effective than in 2008-2009 so far more money must be printed for the same effect.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Expect larger QE programs than prior cycles; key question is where the new money flows (assets vs consumer prices).
insights.quote: They're going to have to to print a lot more money to have the same effect

insights.claim: Frisby distinguishes how QE transmits: post-2008 money printing inflated financial assets, while COVID-era money handed directly to people (plus supply-chain failures) drove consumer price inflation.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Track the delivery channel of new stimulus: bank/bond buying favors asset prices, direct transfers favor CPI and real goods.
insights.quote: After 2008, the inflation we saw was largely in financial assets.

insights.claim: Frisby predicts mandated bond buying and financial repression to cap yields, citing the UK where pension funds and insurers are pushed into gilts, the Bank of England already owns roughly 25-30% of gilts, and savings interest is taxed while gilt returns get favorable tax treatment.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Financial repression suppresses yields below true inflation; watch for US analogs in regulatory mandates for Treasury buying.
insights.quote: I think at the moment it's something like 25 30% of guilts are already owned by the bank of England

insights.claim: Frisby argues the more bond buying is mandated rather than freely chosen, the less yields reflect true inflation, which benefits gold, silver and other traditional hedges.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Financial repression is a direct bullish catalyst for precious metals.
insights.quote: the more gold and silver um and other traditional hedges will benefit

insights.claim: Brent Johnson argues a currency cannot hyperinflate when foreign demand for it exceeds domestic demand, which is why all other fiat currencies will fail before the US dollar does.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Expect USD strength relative to other fiat currencies during global stress; avoid shorting the dollar on US-debt-crisis narratives alone.
insights.quote: you you cannot have hyperinflation of a currency when there's more demand for the currency outside the domestic economy than there is inside the domestic economy

insights.claim: Johnson says gold and the dollar are not mortal enemies: gold will likely rise alongside the dollar, and the dollar does not need to fall or fail for gold to go higher.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Gold can be owned alongside a strong-dollar view; do not treat DXY strength as a reason to sell gold.
insights.quote: the dollar does not have to fall for gold to go higher and the dollar does not have to fail for gold to go higher

insights.claim: Johnson sees US dollar stablecoins as a tool extending the dollar's life: citizens of countries with weaker currencies voluntarily adopt them, stripping monetary sovereignty from local governments and accreting power to the US.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is a structural source of offshore dollar and Treasury demand; watch emerging-market currency pressure as adoption grows.
insights.quote: that then steals monetary sovereignty from those local governments and this power accretes to the United States

insights.claim: Johnson notes that 99% of stablecoins are US dollar stablecoins despite gold and euro stablecoins existing, and that the US government co-opted private crypto rails originally built to bypass the traditional system.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Market share data supports dollar dominance in digital rails; alternative-currency stablecoins have not gained traction.
insights.quote: 99% of stable coins are US dollar stable coins

insights.claim: Peter Schiff counters that nothing tied to an unstable dollar can be stable, predicting the future of stablecoins belongs to gold and that tokenization will ultimately favor tokenized gold over tokenized dollars.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Contrarian long-term case for tokenized gold; adoption depends on accelerating dollar depreciation.
insights.quote: Once you're going to tokenize, you might as well tokenize gold.

insights.claim: Schiff says gold stablecoins will thrive only once dollar depreciation accelerates to monthly/weekly/daily inflation rates that make merchants reluctant to accept dollars; until then dollars work as a medium of exchange and savers should just hold physical gold.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Treat gold-payment rails as an option on high inflation; in the meantime physical gold is the savings vehicle.
insights.quote: That's when you're going to see the big demand for an alternative, and that's when gold stable coins will thrive.

insights.claim: Schiff is promoting T-Gold accounts at Schiff Gold that let users send and receive payments directly in gold, arguing technology allows people to adopt a private gold standard without government.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: Product to watch as a test of gold-as-medium-of-exchange demand; note speaker's commercial interest.

insights.claim: Frisby recounts that in 2015 his team nearly launched a gold stablecoin with Sharps Pixley but abandoned it, and is glad because there are now more than 200 gold stablecoins and essentially nobody uses them; the market has chosen dollars.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence against near-term gold-stablecoin adoption; be skeptical of gold-token investment theses.
insights.quote: there are more than 200 of them and nobody uses them

insights.claim: Frisby says that despite its flaws the dollar has achieved total currency supremacy in the stablecoin world, and he agrees stablecoins will help the US 'drink other countries' milkshake'.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Panel consensus (Johnson, Frisby, Gray) leans toward stablecoins reinforcing USD dominance.
insights.quote: It is the currency that has total currency supremacy.

insights.claim: Frisby believes UK and European policymakers are barely focused on the threat dollar stablecoins pose to their currencies, still discussing CBDCs and worrying more about rates.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Lack of policy response could let dollar stablecoin penetration proceed unchecked in Europe.

insights.claim: Schiff argues the US gets a pass via reflexive safe-haven flows despite having larger debt-to-GDP and budget deficits than many troubled countries such as France, plus a massive trade deficit and being the world's largest debtor nation, and that it will eventually 'hang' with that rope.
insights.speaker: Peter Schiff
insights.so_what: The dollar's safe-haven bid is fragile in his view; a loss of confidence would hit USD and Treasuries simultaneously.
insights.quote: we owe more money than all the other debtor nations of the world combined

insights.claim: Frisby's long-term price comparison since 1970 shows the GBP/USD rate falling from $2.40 to about $1.30 per pound, meaning inflation has been roughly twice as bad in the UK and Western Europe as in the US.
insights.speaker: Dominic Frisby
insights.so_what: Supports a relative-debasement framework: weaker fiat currencies lose purchasing power faster, favoring USD over GBP/EUR.

insights.claim: Russ Gray's 'good ship fiat' framework: all fiat currencies are sinking because of debt, and as weaker ones fail capital crowds into the dollar at the bow, which lasts longer but still goes down.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Dollar strength and long-run fiat decline can coexist; hold real assets while expecting USD to outperform other fiat.

insights.claim: Gray identifies three sources of dollar demand (network effect, dollar-denominated debt, and taxes payable in dollars) and lists the triggers to watch for a breakdown: abolishing the IRS/tax-based demand, a viable de-dollarized global commerce network, or debt reaching a point of no return where borrowing funds interest payments.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Monitor de-dollarization rails and the interest-expense doom loop as signposts for the end of dollar supremacy.
insights.quote: You get to the point where you're borrowing to pay the interest on the debt that you've borrowed. And that's like the doom loop black hole.

insights.claim: Gray argues compounding debt drives ongoing demand for the currency it is denominated in until debt forces a reset, which he believes is much closer now than 10 years ago.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Short-term dollar demand persists, but prepare for an eventual monetary reset.

insights.claim: Russ Gray argues productivity is the key variable that can slow the debt reckoning, and that AI could make the economy far more productive than the internet did, based on widespread Main Street adoption.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: AI-driven productivity is the main bull-case offset to the debt spiral; watch adoption-led productivity data.

insights.claim: Gray cites Google's free cash flow of minus $9 billion in one quarter as evidence that AI capex is absorbing all profits and part of revenue, likening it to paying a deferred bill for technology gains that were previously masked by inflation.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler free cash flow is under heavy pressure from capex; watch FCF trends for AI-spend sustainability.
insights.quote: Look at Google just free cash flow minus 9 billion in one quarter.

insights.claim: Gray, relaying Peter Boockvar, suggests avoiding AI builders (which may not survive, like the Empire State Building's original financiers) and instead favoring companies that use AI to improve their businesses.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Tilt AI exposure toward adopters/beneficiaries rather than capex-heavy infrastructure builders.
insights.quote: I'd be careful about investing in the AI companies because they're probably not going to make it, but the people who use the AI to improve their businesses, those are the companies you should be looking at.

insights.claim: Russ Gray argues currency is not capital but merely a claim on it; real and productive assets (goods, services, income-producing real estate) will become more valuable and should be owned regardless of the currency.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Favor productive real assets whose income adjusts to any currency over cash and paper claims.
insights.quote: I think currency is not capital my opinion. I I think real things are capital and currency is just a claim on that.

insights.claim: Gray points to central banks, the insiders closest to currency, steadily accumulating gold as a signal that gold has a future role in the monetary system.
insights.speaker: Russ Gray
insights.so_what: Central bank gold buying is a structural demand pillar worth tracking.

insights.claim: Brent Johnson considers equities hard assets because they own buildings and inventory and produce real things, making them a good way to outpace fiat dilution, alongside gold which everyone should own.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Pair equities with a core gold position as an anti-debasement portfolio.
insights.quote: I think everybody should own gold

insights.claim: Johnson expects the dollar to keep dominating other fiat currencies and gold to go much higher in coming years, but with volatility, summarizing the alternatives as Europe a museum with a war on its doorstep, Japan an old folks home without energy, and China a prison.
insights.speaker: Brent Johnson
insights.so_what: Relative-attractiveness argument for US assets and USD vs Europe, Japan and China; expect a volatile gold uptrend.
insights.quote: Europe is basically a museum with a war on its doorstep. Japan is an old folks home without an energy supply. And China is a prison.
